title: Slices and maps: len/cap, append, aliasing, nil maps, comma-ok
summary: A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) over an array, so slicing shares memory and append may or may not. A map returns the zero value for missing keys, tells you with comma-ok, and iterates in random order.

examples.title: Slices share their backing array until append runs out of room

annotations.note: arr[1:3] copies nothing: s points at arr[1], has length 2, and capacity 4 because arr has four elements from index 1 on.
Writes through s land in arr. append with spare capacity writes into the same array too, overwriting arr[3], which other code may still be using.
Two more elements don't fit, so append allocates a new array and copies. From then on s and arr are independent. Whether append copied depends on capacity, not on anything visible at the call.
The classic bug: a and b both append into base's spare capacity, so the second append overwrites the first. a[3] is 2, not 1.
base[:3:3] sets capacity to 3, so each append must copy and a and b get their own arrays. slices.Clone(base) is the other way out.

examples.title: Maps: comma-ok, key normalization, random order, nil maps

annotations.note: A missing key yields the zero value, not an exception or undefined. The second result, ok, is the only way to tell "stored 0" from "not there".

Keys are compared byte for byte, so case-insensitive keys need a normalized form. strings.ToLower maps ILIK to ilik, merging lukewarm with bone marrow; unicode.TurkishCase maps I to ı and İ to i, which is right for Turkish text and wrong for English.
fmt sorts map keys when printing (since Go 1.12), which is why this output is stable. That says nothing about range.
The runtime randomizes iteration order on purpose, so code that depends on it breaks in tests instead of after an upgrade. slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) (Go 1.23) gives a stable order.
A nil map behaves like an empty one for reads, len, delete and range, but storing into it panics. A struct with a map field needs a constructor or a lazy make.

examples.title: Passing slices to functions, range copies, nil vs empty

annotations.note: The slice header is copied into the parameter, but it points at the caller's array, so element writes are visible to the caller.
append changes the parameter's length (and maybe its pointer); the caller's header is untouched. If the caller's slice had spare capacity, the new element even lands in its array, invisibly.
Return the slice, exactly like append: xs = add(xs, 4). The compiler rejects a bare append(xs, 4) whose result is unused.
The range value is a copy of each element. To change elements, index: for i := range xs { xs[i] *= 10 }.
A nil slice and an empty one both have length 0 and work with range and append. They differ in == nil and in encoding/json, which writes null for nil and [] for empty; API clients often care.

use_cases: Slices: every ordered collection, buffers, results of queries, function arguments of variable length
Maps: lookups by key, counting, grouping, de-duplication; map[K]struct{} as a set
Full slice expression or slices.Clone: handing out part of a slice that the receiver may append to
Sorted keys of a map: stable output for logs, tests, golden files and APIs
strengths: Slicing is O(1) and copies nothing, unlike Python's or JavaScript's slice, which copy
comma-ok separates a missing key from a stored zero value without exceptions (Python's KeyError) or undefined
Zero values are usable: a nil slice can be appended to and ranged over, a nil map can be read, so empty collections need no setup in most code
Randomized map order makes order-dependent code fail early, in tests, unlike Java's HashMap whose order merely happens to be stable
weaknesses: Whether append shares or copies depends on capacity, so aliasing bugs appear only for some inputs
No ordered map in the standard library; sorted output means sorting the keys
Maps are not safe for concurrent writes: the runtime aborts with 'concurrent map writes'. Use a sync.Mutex or sync.Map
nil and empty slices look the same in Go code but differ in JSON (null vs [])

pitfalls.title: Two appends into one slice's spare capacity
pitfalls.detail: Both results share the array and the second append overwrites the first. Cap the capacity with s[:len(s):len(s)] or copy with slices.Clone before appending.

pitfalls.title: Writing to a nil map in a zero-value struct
pitfalls.detail: var c Cache; c.items["k"] = v panics. Initialize the map in a constructor (NewCache) or with if c.items == nil { c.items = map[string]V{} }.

pitfalls.title: Keeping a small slice of a large array
pitfalls.detail: header := data[:16] keeps the whole data array reachable. Copy what you keep (slices.Clone) when the source is big.

pitfalls.title: Changing a struct stored in a map
pitfalls.detail: m[k].Count++ does not compile (cannot assign to struct field in map): map values are not addressable. Read, modify and store back, or store pointers.

quiz.q: base := make([]int, 3, 10); a := append(base, 1); b := append(base, 2). What is a[3]?
quiz.why: Both appends write index 3 of base's array, which has room. a and b share it, so the second write wins.

quiz.q: m is map[string]int without the key "k". What does v, ok := m["k"] give?
quiz.why: Missing keys yield the zero value; ok reports whether the key was present.

quiz.q: In Python a[1:3] creates a new list. What does a[1:3] create in Go?
options: A slice that shares a's backing array
quiz.why: Slicing builds a new header over the same array; writes through either are visible to both.

quiz.q: var m map[string]int. Which operation panics?
quiz.why: A nil map behaves like an empty read-only map; only storing into it panics.

further_reading.title: Arrays, slices (and strings): The mechanics of 'append'
The Go Programming Language Specification: Slice expressions

body:
## Concept

Go's two built-in collections cover nearly everything. A **slice** `[]T` is a
three-word header: a pointer into an underlying array, a length, and a capacity (how
many elements the array has from that pointer on). Slicing makes a new header over
the same array; `append` writes into the spare capacity when there is some and
allocates a bigger array when there isn't. An array `[N]T` is a fixed-size value that
is copied on assignment, and you rarely use it directly.

A **map** `map[K]V` is a hash table with comparable keys. Reading a missing key
returns the zero value of `V`; `v, ok := m[k]` tells you whether the key was there.
Iteration order is unspecified and deliberately randomized. Maps and slices are both
cheap to pass around: you copy a small header, not the data.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python/JS**: `a[1:3]` and `arr.slice(1, 3)` copy; Go's `a[1:3]` aliases. Python
  dicts and JS `Map` keep insertion order; Go maps keep none.
- **Java**: a slice is like `ArrayList.subList`, a view that writes through, except
  that `append` may silently detach it. A missing map key gives a zero value, not
  `null`, and deleting during `range` is allowed instead of throwing
  `ConcurrentModificationException`.
- **C**: a slice is `struct { T *ptr; size_t len, cap; }` passed by value, and
  `append` is a `realloc` that may move the data. The same rule applies: after a
  possible reallocation, use the returned value.
- **C++**: like `std::vector`, but a sub-slice is a view (`std::span`) that can still
  grow into its parent's storage.

## How it works

```
arr := [5]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
s := arr[1:3]          s = {ptr: &arr[1], len: 2, cap: 4}

arr  [ 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 ]
           ^ s[0]
           |--len--|
           |------cap------|
```

`append(s, x)` checks `len < cap`. If so, it stores `x` at `arr[3]` and returns a
header with `len` 3, same pointer. If not, it allocates a larger array, copies, and
returns a header pointing there. The growth factor is an implementation detail; the
spec only promises a "sufficiently large" array.

## Design notes

Every slice rule follows from "the header is a value, the array is shared". So:
always assign the result of `append`; return slices from functions that grow them;
and when you hand out a slice of your internal state, give a copy (`slices.Clone`) or
cap it (`s[:n:n]`) so the receiver cannot write into your array. Preallocate with
`make([]T, 0, n)` when you know the size. For maps, decide the key's canonical form
before inserting: for user-entered Turkish text that means choosing between
`strings.ToLower` and `strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` based on the
text's language, not the server's locale.

files.examples/01_slice_header.go:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	arr := [5]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5} // an array: fixed length, copied on assignment
	s := arr[1:3]                // a slice: pointer into arr, len 2, cap 4
	fmt.Println(s, len(s), cap(s))

	s[0] = 20 // writes through to arr
	fmt.Println("arr:", arr)

	s = append(s, 30) // room left in cap: append overwrites arr[3]
	fmt.Println("arr:", arr)

	s = append(s, 40, 50) // no room: new backing array, arr is left alone
	s[0] = 99
	fmt.Println("arr:", arr, "s:", s)

	// The classic bug: two appends to the same slice share its spare capacity.
	base := make([]int, 3, 10)
	a := append(base, 1)
	b := append(base, 2)
	fmt.Println("a:", a, "b:", b)

	// A full slice expression base[low:high:max] caps the capacity, so the
	// next append has to copy.
	a = append(base[:3:3], 1)
	b = append(base[:3:3], 2)
	fmt.Println("a:", a, "b:", b)
}
